explanations.explanation: Close, baker, but Jesus doesn't ask for a trip across the lake. He asks Simon "…to put out a little from shore." (Luke 5:3). That's just enough distance to sit down and teach the crowd from the boat. Think of it as a floating stage with a fisherman for a stagehand.

Right, baker. Jesus asks Simon "…to put out a little from shore." (Luke 5:3). He doesn't ask for a trip across the lake. The crowd stays right there on the shore, and Jesus teaches them from the boat. A little way out, and everybody can still hear.
You got it, baker. "And sitting down, He taught the people from the boat." (Luke 5:3). Luke 5:2 says the fishermen were washing their nets. Now Simon's boat is where the teaching happens.

Not here, baker. Luke 5:3 says Jesus sat down and "…taught the people from the boat." The text doesn't mention any healing in this scene. This boat is all about teaching, and the crowd gets a front-row seat from the shore.

Not this time, friend. Luke 5:3 says that sitting in the boat, Jesus "…taught the people…" There's no baptizing in this scene. I'm guessing the water just made the boat feel like a good place for it. The text says teaching, though, so teaching it is.

explanations.answer: We worked hard all night and caught nothing
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Simon says, "we have worked hard all night without catching anything." (Luke 5:5). That's a whole night of work with nothing to show for it. I've had a rough batch or two myself, and Simon's night was way bigger than that.

explanations.answer: We sold our whole catch before sunrise
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend, not yet anyway. Simon says they "…worked hard all night without catching anything." (Luke 5:5). That night gave them nothing to sell. A big catch does come later in the passage (Luke 5:6), but only after Jesus speaks.

explanations.answer: A storm kept us on shore all night
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. Simon doesn't mention any storm. He says they "…worked hard all night without catching anything." (Luke 5:5). What he tells Jesus about is hard work and no fish.

That's it, baker. Simon says, "But because You say so, I will let down the nets." (Luke 5:5). After a night like that, I'd have OPINIONS about letting those nets down again. Simon gives one reason, and it's what Jesus said.

explanations.answer: Because the fish move at daybreak
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, but Simon doesn't give that reason. He says, "But because You say so, I will let down the nets." (Luke 5:5). I'd love a fish forecast too, but Simon doesn't hand one out.

explanations.answer: Because his partners ask him to
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Jesus is the one who tells Simon, "Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch." (Luke 5:4). Simon answers, "But because You say so, I will let down the nets." (Luke 5:5). His reason is what Jesus said, not a request from his partners.

Oh, baker, no. Not this time. When Simon and the others let the nets down, "…they caught such a large number of fish that their nets began to tear." (Luke 5:6). Empty was last night. This time the nets are so full they start to rip.
YES, baker! After a whole night of nothing, "…they caught such a large number of fish that their nets began to tear." (Luke 5:6). Nothing all night, and then nets ripping. Talk about a turnaround!

You got it, baker. "…they signaled to their partners in the other boat to come and help them…" (Luke 5:7). The nets are tearing, so they wave over the other boat. Then both boats get filled so full that they begin to sink.

Close, but not the word, baker. Luke 5:7 says they signaled "…to their partners in the other boat…" Later we learn two of those partners are James and John, the sons of Zebedee (Luke 5:10). Partners, not servants.

Not quite, friend. The text says they signaled "…to their partners in the other boat to come and help them…" (Luke 5:7). Partners are the ones who share the work. Nobody's waving over the folks next door.
Yes, baker. They "…filled both boats so full that they began to sink." (Luke 5:7). That's so many fish that two boats can barely stay up. I'd say that's the kind of problem a fisherman dreams about.
Not quite, baker. Luke 5:7 says the boats were filled "…so full that they began to sink." Drifting would be the calm version. This is a lot more dramatic, with two boats riding low in the water.
Ha, that would be something to see, baker. But Luke 5:7 says they filled both boats "…so full that they began to sink." No spinning here. The boats are just loaded down with fish.
That's right, baker. Luke 5:8 says, "When Simon Peter saw this, he fell at Jesus’ knees." The boats are so full they're beginning to sink. What Simon Peter does is drop down in front of Jesus.
Good thinking, baker, but that's not what happens. Luke 5:8 says Simon Peter "…fell at Jesus’ knees." His focus goes to Jesus, not to his gear.

explanations.answer: He runs to tell the crowd
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Simon Peter doesn't go anywhere. He "…fell at Jesus’ knees." (Luke 5:8). He's still right there in the boat, down in front of Jesus.

explanations.answer: Go away from me Lord because I'm a sinful man
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Simon Peter says, "Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man" (Luke 5:8). Luke 5:9 says he and his companions were astonished at the catch of fish. I think this is a heavy moment for him, and I'd just let his words stand.

explanations.answer: Stay with me Lord because I need Your help
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd pick that, baker, but those aren't his words. Simon Peter says, "Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man" (Luke 5:8). He asks Jesus to go away, and he gives his reason: he is a sinful man.

explanations.answer: Teach me Lord how to find fish like that
explanations.explanation: Fair guess, baker, since the fish are the big news. But Simon Peter says, "Go away from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man" (Luke 5:8). He's not asking for tips. He's talking about himself.

Yes, baker. Simon, his companions and his partners James and John are astonished at the catch, and Jesus says to Simon, "Do not be afraid…" (Luke 5:9-10). Simon had just fallen at His knees, so those words land right where he is. Short, plain and kind.

Not quite, baker. Simon, his companions and his partners James and John are astonished at the catch (Luke 5:9-10). Jesus does speak to Simon, and He says, "Do not be afraid…" (Luke 5:10). He says it plainly to Simon.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, "From now on you will catch men." (Luke 5:10). Simon is out fishing, and Jesus tells him what's ahead. The words "From now on…" tell us it's a new start.
Not quite, friend. Jesus tells Simon, "From now on you will catch men." (Luke 5:10). Tax collecting doesn't come up in this passage. Simon is a fisherman, and Jesus speaks in fishing terms.
Close to the water, baker, but no. Jesus says, "From now on you will catch men." (Luke 5:10). Simon isn't headed to a boatyard. He's headed toward something new that Jesus describes.
Not what the text says, baker. After they brought the boats ashore, "…they left everything and followed Him." (Luke 5:11). Nobody stays behind to sell the catch. They walk away from all of it.
You've got it, baker. "…when they had brought their boats ashore, they left everything and followed Him." (Luke 5:11). Nobody hangs around to sell the catch. They leave it all and go after Jesus.
